title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
content:

Title:On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:On-policy reinforcement learning for large language models assumes that training responses are sampled from the current policy. In practice, an inference engine samples the responses and a separate trainer computes the gradients, and the \textbf{training-inference mismatch} between the two makes the training data off-policy. The mismatch has two sources, the numerics of the engine and the stale weights of asynchronous sampling, and a correction that stabilizes training under one source can fail under the other. \textit{We ask which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs.} Evaluating the trainer at the sampler's weights splits each sampled-token error exactly into a \textit{numerical discrepancy} of the engine and a \textit{policy lag} of the trainer, and we follow both through training. The numerical discrepancy stays approximately constant, so it biases the updates by a nearly fixed amount, and centering the score at each prefix removes its leading bias. The policy lag is produced by the trainer's own updates: the bias it leaves enters the next update, which enlarges the next lag and closes a feedback loop. Importance weighting cuts this loop only while the lag ratio stays concentrated, and on Qwen3-1.7B it fails at the step where the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half. From this account we derive the \textbf{discrepancy-lag correction} (DLC), which centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler's weights and resynchronizes the sampler when this effective sample size falls below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy trainings on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and its resynchronization prevents collapses that the per-token corrections leave and that a KL measured on the sampler's prefixes does not detect.

report.summary: A new analysis disentangles numerical engine error from stale-weight policy lag in LLM reinforcement learning, yielding a correction that stabilizes asynchronous training.
report.background: On-policy reinforcement learning for large language models assumes training responses come from the current policy. In practice, a fast inference engine such as vLLM or SGLang samples responses, while a separate trainer such as FSDP or Megatron computes gradients. Asynchronous sampling improves throughput but makes data off-policy because engine numerics differ and sampler weights go stale. Prior fixes, including importance weighting and clipping, often treat the mismatch as one problem. This paper asks which property of a mismatch source determines the correction it needs. The question matters as RL post-training scales and rollout generation becomes a major bottleneck, making training-inference consistency a central systems and algorithm issue.
key_points: The paper separates training-inference mismatch into two sources: numerical discrepancy from the inference engine and policy lag from stale sampler weights. These behave differently. Numerical discrepancy stays roughly constant and creates a nearly fixed bias, while policy lag feeds back into training and can grow over time.

The authors evaluate the trainer at the sampler's weights to split each sampled-token error into numerical discrepancy and policy lag. This decomposition lets them track how each source evolves and shows why a correction that stabilizes one source can fail under the other.

Importance weighting only controls policy lag while the lag ratio remains concentrated. On Qwen3-1.7B it fails when the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half, showing that per-token corrections alone are not enough for stale samplers.

The proposed discrepancy-lag correction, DLC, centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler's weights, and resynchronizes the sampler when effective sample size drops below one half. This combines per-token fixes with a system-level reset.

On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, DLC keeps KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy runs. Its resynchronization also prevents collapses that per-token corrections leave behind and that prefix-based KL does not detect.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the work reframes asynchronous RL stability as two distinct problems rather than one, which could make high-throughput post-training systems more reliable. Developers building RLHF or reasoning-model pipelines should monitor effective sample size, separate engine numerics from policy lag, and consider periodic sampler resynchronization instead of relying only on importance weighting or clipping. This may reduce silent training collapses and wasted GPU hours. For regular users, the practical effect is indirect but important: more stable RL training can produce more reliable models with fewer regressions. The paper also suggests evaluation should not rely solely on KL measured on sampler prefixes, since that can miss failures that DLC's resynchronization catches.
report.tools: Watch vLLM and SGLang for inference-engine numerics, and veRL, OpenRLHF, TRL, and SkyRL for LLM RL training stacks. These frameworks are where DLC-style centering, lag-ratio clipping, effective-sample-size monitoring, and sampler resynchronization would likely be implemented. Also track the paper's authors for code release and check Hugging Face for Qwen3-based reproducibility artifacts.
